memory_candidates.content: When adding artifact-presence-based auto-promotion to a task-state reconciler, artifact PRESENCE alone is not sufficient signal to distinguish a crashed/stranded run from a deliberately-reset task whose old artifacts were restored alongside it (e.g. a recover/restore workflow that moves a whole task directory back and re-stamps a reset timestamp on the same write). Artifact RECENCY relative to the state's last-updated timestamp is a cheap, effective local disambiguator: a crashed run's artifact necessarily postdates the last successful status write, while a restored task's artifacts all predate the reset stamp. Ties must refuse, not permit (strict greater-than, not greater-or-equal), since a directory move can land on the same whole-second mtime. This matters most on unattended/autonomous promotion paths where no human reviews the outcome before it takes effect.

When verifying a bash script change via sandbox execution, self-referential comment text (a header note that says 'see helper_name below') inflates a naive grep -c 'helper_name' count beyond what a plan's stated verification step may anticipate. This is harmless to functional correctness but worth checking for directly (grep -n, not just grep -c) before treating a count mismatch as a real defect.

In a shared repository with multiple concurrent agents committing to agent-system/ (or any shared source tree) simultaneously, a `git add <scoped paths>` followed by `git commit` can appear to fail with 'no changes added to commit' even though the content was genuinely committed -- because a race with another agent's own commit (which staged and committed overlapping working-tree state first) already carried the intended changes into history, just under a different commit message/attribution. Verify via `git log --oneline -- <path>` and `git show <commit>:<path>` diffed against the pre-change baseline, rather than assuming a nonzero exit from `git commit` means data loss.
